utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Flynn, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is hardly any need to say, but you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Kay continues, I will just want to let the court know that we will not be engaging in cross today, and we will give the balance of our time, with the Court's permission, to Mr. Kay or Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not only not today, but not for this witness at all, I take it. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very generous, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, if we can just turn to that document we were trying to find yesterday, where there had been a mix over the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could call up P46, it's a HRAT report dated the 23rd [sic] of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is one of the exhibits that you produced with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still not sure this is a HRAT report. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I call it a HRAT report because in paragraph 4, it mentions HRAT and it came through you. You're known as the HRAT witness, by the way.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it must be a HRAT report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But forgive us for that, it's just a way we organise things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's from Mr. Al-Alfi with whom you were working?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You recollect those questions I asked you about the meeting in Plavno on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you see, on paragraph 2 of Exhibit P46, that meeting is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was also to be arranged that Mr. Pasic, the mayor of Knin, would be there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at this time, Mr. Romanic informed the HRAT - not meaning that you're that HRAT, but your organisation - that most of the police efforts are focussing on patrolling remote areas?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that your experience of the civil police at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As Mr. Romanic put it, "in order to locate and protect the remaining population," was that your experience?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That he said that they were doing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was your experience -- whether you noticed that that was happening?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not notice a significant patrolling presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2 of this document, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We had a discussion yesterday about the police stations opening, and remember I produced the document that showed the list of police stations which were ordered to open or to be set up from the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you said, "I doubt whether they were in place by then, and it would have been much later before they were effective."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, we see that Mr. Romanic mentioned Gracac, Donji Lapac, Korenica, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Stankovac "are now opened." So it seems that you were right, that there was a period of time before they were opened for business?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 6, a man called Mr. Jukic Pavo, a chemistry engineer normally based in civil defence headquarters in Zagreb, is now in charge of the civil defence in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Jukic Pavo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to what did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, in relation to this matter of the collection of dead bodies and the situation at the Knin cemetery. I'm not sure if I met him on this occasion, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Presumably, in the course of your business, you met people in a large number of different meetings and contexts --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- would that be right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, Mr. Jukic gave figures of about 130 bodies being buried by that time in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By "Knin area," it's clarified here as meaning all of them in Knin cemetery and according to international standards. Was that something that you had a discussion with him or a meeting with him about, the form and nature of burials being in accordance with international standards?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that came up in our discussions. We were certainly paying attention to what was taking place at the cemetery, to the number of persons who were being buried there and to the procedures followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that the deputy prime minister, Mr. Kostovic, was the only person who was allowed to speak in public on this matter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you have any discussions with Mr. Kostovic about the matter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we take it, from the terms of your evidence yesterday, that you didn't go higher than the local regional area for dealing with these problems, that ministers and more senior people either did not make themselves available to you or you were unable to speak to them? Was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And I considered that my responsibility was in the former Sector South, and that discussions with more senior officials would take place in Zagreb with my colleagues there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That leads me on to ask: What the structure was in Zagreb? What was the nature of other colleagues that you had there? What was the set-up for dealing with these bigger issues, perhaps, which couldn't be dealt with on the ground?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our reports went to many different locations, I think; but for our purposes, they went to the humanitarian crisis cell which was a structure in the office of the special representative of the Secretary General, which had responsibility obviously for dealing with humanitarian issues and human rights issues. And our reports also went to the office of the Centre for Human Rights in Zagreb where there were about four or five staff. And one reason that I left the Knin area for a few days was to meet with my colleagues up there, discuss follow-up, sort of give them a briefing firsthand as to what was going on in Sector South -- former Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to turn now to the visit to Grubori on the 25th of August; and yesterday or the day before, you produced document P27.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If that could be called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm calling it up now to give you an opportunity to refresh your memory, as it's been a little while since you've addressed these issues in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You will recollect that in the second paragraph of section 2, that that afternoon, at 1630 hours, you went to General Cermak's office where that office was informed of the fire and the needs of the homeless residents.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, you spoke there to an English-speaking person within the office?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it was Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dondo's reaction to that information was what?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, he expressed concern, he expressed appreciation for the report, and he indicated that the matter would be followed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. With you on that particular mission to Grubori, were what other agencies from the UN?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that visit that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNHCR, the High Commissioner for Refugees, there was a participant from UN CIVPOL, and I believe there was a participant from the political and humanitarian affairs office of the sector of UNCRO in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. You had gone from Grubori back to Knin to make this report at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the length of time that it took to make that journey at that time - I don't mean now in present conditions, but at that time when things were probably slightly different - was how long, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I don't recall now how long, but I would say maybe 40 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And having returned to Knin, did anyone report what had been seen at Grubori to the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure we went to the police station. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you stay together as a group or did any of the group in Knin split up? Perhaps the UN CIVPOL man may have gone to the police station, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not sure. I'm having trouble recalling that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. But the report was made to Mr. Dondo. On that particular day, the 25th of August, am I right that it was a -- the weather was bad on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The decision was made by you and your colleagues to go back to Grubori that very same evening?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was on that second visit that you discovered two murdered people?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see the report of that in the section of the paragraph below 1630.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Grubori on that second visit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say probably about an hour to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. What sort of times are we talking about as when you arrived for the second visit and what time had you left by?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, and, of course, I'm estimating now because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not tying you -- don't think that there's any -- it's just for information.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was probably about 5.30 or 6.00 in the afternoon that we got back there, and we would have left around 7.00, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Returning, presumably, straight back to Knin or did you go anywhere else after you'd left Grubori?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We went straight back to Knin. We generally tried to avoid being on the roads at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. On that second visit, at the time you were there, were there any investigation authorities or any police there at the scene?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got back to Knin that evening after the second visit, did anyone report the matter to the Knin police?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I suspect that we may have entrusted that responsibility to our UN CIVPOL colleague, but I don't recall that I was a participant in a report to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you can remember his name, your UN CIVPOL representative on this journey, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was something like Romasev, a Russian individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got back to Knin, did you report your further finding of two further bodies to any other agency?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a Croatian agency?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe we did so that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. In relation to that information concerning the two murders, did you pass that on to anyone that evening?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, to UN colleagues, and that would have been it on that evening. Again, I'm not sure if it was reported to the local police by my UN CIVPOL colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, the 26th of August, you didn't return to Grubori as part of that particular visit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But did you acquire further information in the course of that date from your UN colleagues as to their further findings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I learned that three more bodies had been discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you recollect what time it was that you discovered that? I'm looking at the bottom paragraph of P27 Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly, but I would guess late morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, of course, that morning we had no particular expectation that there would be more bodies found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. But there was a further visit back to Grubori by the UN in relation to what they had found the previous date?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. And there was also a concern about the situation of the people who were still living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And that had, in fact, been the purpose of the scheduled meeting on the previous day, the 25th.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we turn now, please, to 65 ter 4473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes D57, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a Prosecution Exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have the document yet on the screen; and perhaps if Mr. Kay can indicate what tab, I could follow on my hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not a tab on the hard copy. It's a big document. It's the Knin police station record book from -- for August 1995 during the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on our screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have the front page. It's from the 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see it, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During the uploading of this document, I was advised that it was a big document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 234 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So we've put an extract in, Your Honour, but anyone is welcome to look at anything else. I dare say that the whole of the book will eventually go into evidence, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case then perhaps we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, take a moment. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page after this, and I can see what the situation was in relation to the uploading of this document, whether the whole document was done? They've done the whole document, so can we go to page 59, page 59 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What we are going to be looking at is the extract from the Knin police station book, Mr. Flynn --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- for the 26th of August, 1995, and it's before you now. The original handwritten version is on the right; translated typed version on the left.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The book was handwritten by the operatives in the police station, obviously. We will see, at point 193, under the date 26th of August, 1995, at the time of 1500, commander of the 1st police station, Milos Mihic. First of all, did you have meetings or dealings with Mr. Mihic, who was the commander of the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Name and family name of the employee who received report on the incident. Someone named Begonja is listed who was probably the station sergeant or officer for that day. We see a report on a body. He reported verbally that information had been received, that in Plavno village, Grubori hamlet, on 25th of August, 1995, two male bodies were found: Milos Grubar, born 1915; and Jovan Grubar, 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Would the "he" refer to Mr. Begonja?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would say it's Mr. Mihic actually, looking at this document and having seen that Mr. Begonja is the recording officer, so it came from Mr. Mihic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Others can, if they disagree with that, can advance a point, but sometimes these things can be seen. Then you will see a comment: "It was agreed with Chief Cedo Romanic that an on site investigation would be conducted in the morning of 27th of August, 1995. Civilian protection went to the scene at 1100 hours on the 27th of August, 1995, and removed the bodies." And we see on the right the name Begonja.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, were you aware that this matter was advised to the Knin police station by the commander, Mr. Mihic, on the 26th at 1500?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And by 1500, it would seem that the UN, at least, had known that there were five bodies of murdered people in that village.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please check whether the -- what we see in the original and what we see is the translation, is that the same page or is that -- because for those who try to follow it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It doesn't look like it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if those who are following these proceedings in the original language want to look at the screen, then they see something quite different from what we are discussing in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In the Croatian document, you will need to put in number 192 - we're on 189 - to get that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So three pages further down, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're on the right page now, Your Honour, but we've gone down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that we are now approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in view of the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Zoom out so that those who want to follow it in the original language can see approximately what we see in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's leave, I will leave perhaps a couple of seconds for people just to digest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the reporting system to the civil police that I now want to ask you about, Mr. Flynn. What was the procedure when you found a crime during your research? During your tours of the region, what was to happen, what was supposed to happen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, I'm recalling now that there was a special professional relationship between UN CIVPOL and the Croatian police. I think, yesterday, we discussed this practice whereby an important part of the duties of UN CIVPOL was to actually work with the Croatian police and monitor in a way what they were doing, and that was a regular line of communication between UN CIVPOL and the Croatian police. So I'm quite confident that UN CIVPOL would have referred this information to the Croatian police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that the commander was advised by UN CIVPOL, Mr. Mihic, and that's why he made this record at 1500.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It may not be the time that the information got to him, but that's the time it's recorded --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to be fair to the system, perhaps. But there we have it. We have two bodies recorded at that time. If we go to the next page of the book, page 60, there are further events recorded in the book, which we don't need to look at in detail on this occasion, but it just shows how the book is compiled. Then we go to page 61, incident 197 of Exhibit D57. And we see at 197, 26th of August, 1995 at 2000, Croatian army officer Dondo Karolj?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Damir Vrkic who received report of the incident, and then we see a short description of the report: "Report on bodies in Plavno village, Grubori hamlet. There are five bodies of men and women who were killed during military and police Operation Storm." And it was taken over by Begonja. And in the next paragraph, "Information on this will subsequently be passed on to civilian protection officers for hygiene and sanitation measures," 27th of August, 1995. And we know now who Karolj Dondo is because you've told us he is the liaison officer with whom you had dealings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think the witness quite said that Karolj, Dondo was the person with whom the witness had dealings with. It was suggested to the witness that the person he spoke to was Karolj, Dondo on the 25th, and the witness agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's verify with the witness and see whether that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, we've rather looked at him in more detail now, and his name and persona has come through in the last few days. You remember you suddenly recollected when I put the name to you. He spoke English, not fluently. You spoke to him on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember now what his role was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, he was often with General Cermak. I referred to him as a deputy, but I meant that not in a formal sense but in the sense that he was some sort of a senior assistant to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are documents that show his role in the Croatian army, so don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That deals with those questions that I wanted to -- no. Just a few more questions I may be able to ask you about this. Did you go on the 27th of August to Grubori? There were a large number of people that visited on the 27th, and there was a film of it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go back to Grubori at all after the 25th? Yes, because you looked at the bullet casing, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was something like the first week of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was ten days later?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that your first visit back?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. So I can't ask you any further about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning now to a new subject, Your Honour, concerning the reporting of matters in September of 1995 arising from Her Honour's questions on Exhibit P38 while the evidence was given from the witness on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Presidents, I just wish to point out that I have no objections to the admission of the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was D57 and is therefore admitted into evidence. That's the long report, the full 234 pages, police records. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we bring up on to the screen 65 ter 2681.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D58, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This, again, is a document arising from the 65 ter list, Your Honour. Can it formally be produced as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for Ms. Mahindaratne to report whether there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Then D58 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, we have almost all of the documents we see on the screen is all draft translations which, of course, is of some concern to me. Could I earlier urge the parties to see whether we could get final translations rather than draft translations or translations still to be revised? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A criminal report on the 5th of September, 1995. I'm going to look at a collection of criminal reports around just after this date between the 5th and the 8th, and then look at a much bigger report, Mr. Flynn, so it's for informative purposes concerning that issue that was being raised.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This criminal report from the 72nd police -- Military Police Battalion of Knin. Page 2, reporting of a crime on the 2nd of September, 1995, we see at the top of the page, the crime of aggravated theft. At the foot of the page, we see what that was, something to do with a steam boiler and radiator, and on page 3 that he was stopped by the military police. And in the middle of page 3, the conclusion by the commander, Colonel Butimir, that there is reason to suspect that he committed the act he has been charged with. So that criminal report was going to the military Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Was the subject of this described as a civilian or -- I didn't see the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the first page, he's a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for the interruption. I just wanted to clarify that you had raised the issue of the draft translation, and we would challenge the translation of the -- of that last paragraph, because it is a little confusing to say -- if you could bring me back to the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First page, last page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Second page, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Obviously, from a legal perspective - the last paragraph of the document, please - where he says, "Based ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says, "There is reason to suspect that he really did commit the act for which he has been charged."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's not been charged yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think, in the Croatian, it really should be translated more as, "There is reason to suspect that he committed the act of which he stands suspected or accused."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not my translation. It's the fact of the report that we're looking at, Your Honour, but the concern over the accuracy does remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But I'm not relying on the content; it's the fact, as the think the Court will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic is emphasising or aligning that there are -- that the final translation might be different from the draft translation; therefore, we have to be very careful. At the same time, you are not, at this time, focussing on the content of the report and the details there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll let you finish this first report and then see whether this is the way in which we should deal with it. It depends on what the witness knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. What I was going to do, Your Honour, was put in a collection of reports that show a number of charges that have been brought in the days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you expect that the witness has any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then why inform the witness, where apparently the first thing which should be done is to inform the Court about these matters? Is there any way, Ms. Mahindaratne, that you could agree that you say, well, both parties agree that there do exist so many reports dealing with theft of a steam boiler, so that we get a kind of a brief, perhaps, attached to all of the reports, but that the Chamber is informed about what Mr. Kay now through this witness apparently wants to establish that police reports were made. I'm not going any step further whether these police reports, what the following-up has been, but just that such reports were made and that we'll know whether it's about steam boilers, whether it's about trucks, whether it's about hand-held rockets that were stolen, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that we get the information. Why do we need to spend hours with the witness on this matter. Mr. Mr. Kay, I'm addressing you, and addressing you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I did discuss this with Mr. Kay yesterday; and even the documents that were tendered yesterday, I believe can be tendered through a bar table motion simply because the witness is not aware of most of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there is no -- we do not contest most of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber suggest to the parties that this set of police reports are put in one bundle, that we get a cover page which says number one, that place, that date, this is the suspicion; that is, in this case, steam boiler and radiator being stolen. Then we don't have to ask the witness whether he's aware of these reports, then he answers that he's not aware of these reports, and then they are admitted into evidence. There is a more effective, more efficient way of doing that. Are you confident, Ms. Mahindaratne, and you, Mr. Kay, that in this way, the Chamber could receive the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, I was going to do this very rapidly, and it was to assist the Bench because of the question a couple of days ago. There is a document of at the end of this little collection that I've got, which is 65 ter 2999, which is a report from the Zadar Knin police station, police administration, for the attention of the administration chief dated the 6th of September, 1995, which actually outlines the murders that they say they investigated and other crimes. And this was to illuminate this point in a quick way; and, of course, the only way I have, when I'm here, is through a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the traditional, I would say, common law approach, which is not necessary. The Chamber is always open for efficient other ways of receiving evidence, especially if there is no challenge to the existence of those documents. I mean, if the witness doesn't know anything about it, he can't tell us whether they are authentic or not. He cannot tell us whether any follow-up was given, whether the content was accurately reflecting what was the result of investigations, but at least that these reports apparently were produced at that time. I think we can do that without a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, as I suggested yesterday to Mr. Kay, what I suggested was that we be served with the documents that the Defence intends to tender in evidence, and I would just agree to all those documents. But we still haven't got some of the documents that Mr. Kay intends to tender into evidence this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if we are talking about the existence of police reports on which Mr. Flynn could not give any further clarification, then there are other and more efficient ways in getting that to -- into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just turn now to 65 ter 2261; tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This, again, arises from that information given on the 7th of September in the Exhibit P38, and concerns a statement by Mr. Cermak. You can see it there: "There is no place for looters in the Croatian army." And according to Colonel-General Ivan Cermak, commander of the Knin assembly point: "A large scale operation has been launched to resolve problems related to the illegal appropriation of apartments and looting, torching homes, acts regrettably most often committed by members of the Croatian army. Some ten warrants already been issued for arresting and bringing before the Military Court in Split such soldiers who, as General Cermak stated, defile the Croatian Army and have no place in it." Referring to a text published in a newspaper, under the headline "Apartment Safari," General Cermak said that: "The claims in the text were completely accurate but that the military and civil police units have been strengthened so as to prevent illegal actions." General Cermak also said that: "The commanders of the units of those troops whose troops commit criminal offences also bear responsibility." That's as much as we need to bring out of that, and this was at the time of your meeting on the 7th of September, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not recall. Did I report on a meeting with General Cermak on the 7th --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, P38.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can look at the document, P38 page 3.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You gave evidence about it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't think I was at that meeting myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's in the HRAT report that you've produced, in which he refers to having informed on a recent interview on Croatian television --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and given statements condemning crimes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I ask about that. Your Honour, that concludes my cross-examination because of the Court's sensible suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kuzmanovic, Mr. Kay took even less time. I'm not asking you to change your mind, but it's only fair, and if you say, I gave some of my time to Mr. Kay, that if you would -- if you are trying to resolve a problem which does not exist in the same way as it appears to exist before, then if you would reconsider your position then we will then consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will not be having any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to point out that the previous document did not get a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It did not get a number. That's the newspaper article, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D59, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you wanted to tell us whether you objected against it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D59 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, will you now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just remark, Your Honour, that in light of your instruction yesterday, I've narrowed down my cross, so we may finish early. I just wanted the Court to be aware that we may actually have extra time this afternoon, in light of that instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no extra -- let me just check now what you said because I might have missed a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can clarify, Your Honour. Yesterday, you told me to be ready to finish by the beginning of the second break, and I suspect I will be finished by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are under less time restraints at this moment, since the Chamber allowed the next witness to be called to go to another place, because that witness is expected to testify on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, we are a little bit less under time restraint. At the same time, an exercise in efficient and effective cross-examination is something that's always good for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's in your statement that you worked -- you came to Croatia in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And at the time, you were working for Mr. Mazowiecki?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was assisting him in his mandate. I wasn't working for him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say, "assisting him in his mandate," how were you assisting him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the Special Rapporteur for the Commission on Human Rights, and he had a mandate to report to the UN commission on the human rights and humanitarian law situation in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. There were five or six international staff who were hired to assist him in gathering facts throughout the region, and I was one of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would that be five or six staff for the entire former Yugoslavia or just Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the entire former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a Croatian military operation known as Operation Flash, which took place in May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How are you familiar with that operation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was also in Croatia when that took place, and I had occasion to go to that area shortly after that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in any interviews of Serbs who remained in the territory of Western Slavonia after Operation Flash was completed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask Mr. Registrar to pull up 1D12-0051, and highlight the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, it would be number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D60, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, we'll blow this up a little bit, but I believe you can see this is a report submitted by the Special Rapporteur, on 5 July 1995, concerning the situation of human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you typically assist Mr. Mazowiecki in preparing these types of reports?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could we go to paragraph 28, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be helpful if it was a little larger, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll read that out for the record at "During the first two ..." This is now discussing Operation Flash, and it says, "During the first two days of the military operation, as many as 10.000 people fled from the Serb-held area of Western Slavonia, mostly from the Okucani area, across the Sava River bridge, into northern Bosnia and Herzegovina. The RSK authorities had previously held regular evacuation drills, and there are reports that some of the refugees may have been forced into leaving against their will." If we could stop there for a moment. Do you have any information as to how Mr. Mazowiecki came to the information that the RSK authorities had previously held regular evacuation drills?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fairly sure he got that from members of my team. I don't remember if I was involved in getting that information myself, but I was responsible for monitoring the situation in that area. So we may well have provided him that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the specific type of information that your team may have had? Were they reports, documents, witnesses?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I just don't recall that. I notice that -- yeah. No, I just don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then it continues on: "And there are reports that some of the refugees may have been forced into leaving against their will." Am I correct to say that from the context of the report, that refers to RSK authorities forcing Serbs into leaving against their will?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall any reports -- let me rephrase that. Do you recall any specific reports that you could recall for the Trial Chamber concerning RSK authorities forcing Serbs to leave against their will?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't right here. I could perhaps do some research. There may have been reports coming from other UN sources in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm just not sure at this time what reports that refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The paragraph goes on: "Subsequently, in negotiations with UNPF," which is UN protection force, "and Croatian authorities, the leaders of the RSK insisted that persons left behind, estimated at 3 to 4.000, be given the opportunity to leave Western Slavonia and join the other refugees in the Serb-held territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The United Nations acceded to this demand, and initiated the programme known as Operation Safe Passage within the context of the Four Point Cessation of Hostilities Agreement." Do you recall a United Nations operation known as Operation Safe Passage?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, not in all its details, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what Operation Safe Passage was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I don't feel I feel fully qualified to describe it with any certainty. It's just been too long. I really wouldn't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, generally, that it was an operation through which the United Nations assisted in moving Serbs from Western Slavonia and into Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can go on to the next paragraph: "Serbs still living in the sector were advised of their right to remain, and the public assurances of the Government of Croatia that their rights, including the right to citizenship of the Republic of Croatia, would be fully respected. Nevertheless, during the month of May, hundreds of Serbs from the Sector West ..." And Sector West is the area of Western Slavonia, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... applied for inclusion in Operation Safe Passage. And by early June, more than 2.000 had left for Serb-held territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to recent information, no more than 1.000 remain in the sector. Numerous observers have voiced concerns that the operation was conducted in an unduly hasty manner and persons were not adequately informed of their rights." If we could stop there for a moment. Do you recall any concerns that were voiced about Operation Safe Passage?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall, generally, that those concerns were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall by whom?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only make a reasoned speculation that it might involve, for example, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees or representatives of NGOs, and some of -- but I'm just not sure who that reference is to, "the numerous observers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can continue on then. It goes on to say: "However, continuing demand for inclusion in the exit convoys as late as mid-June suggest that most Serbs in Western Slavonia were intent upon leaving under any circumstances. Intending refugees interviewed by the Special Rapporteur's field staff indicated that the main reasons for their wish to depart were the desire to join relatives who had already fled and doubts about future prospects in Croatia, especially the security situation and the likelihood of finding work." Mr. Flynn, were you one of the field staff that interviewed these intending refugees referenced in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And where did you hold these interviews?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area. We probably -- I mean, I know that we spoke with Serb residents of Western Slavonia in that area, and I think in some cases in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And when you spoke to them, did you also indicate to them that the government of Croatia was giving them assurances that their rights would be protected if they stayed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what did these people that are indicated in this report as "intending refugees, how did they when you advised them that the government of Croatia was guaranteeing their rights?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was certainly skepticism about that and the people expressed concern over their future prospects, and they did not trust that the Croatian government would fully respect their rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There was a fear among these refugees of the Croatian government; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe not of the government, per se, but whether the government could provide adequate protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to another topic now. I don't know if the Bench has questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- don't worry, we'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could turn now to Operation Storm. You were in Zagreb on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could pull up, Mr. Registrar, 1D12-0083.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit D61, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The UN document, I take it, Ms. Mahindaratne, that there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D61 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, were you aware on the 4th of August that there had been allegations that were in the public domain that the Croatian army had shelled civilian areas in Knin on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the statement that is now in front of you by Mr. Carl Bildt, who you will recall was the representative of the European Union at the time to the international conference on the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall this statement in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You recall, generally, that Carl Bildt had issued a statement on the 4th of August that: "It is difficult to see any difference between the rocket attack by RSK forces on Zagreb in May and the shelling of Knin which President Tudjman must now be held responsible for."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall that I was aware of that statement at that time, but I'm -- I have no doubt about the accuracy of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any reports shortly after the statement was issued whereby the Croatian government declared Mr. Bildt to be personae non gratae as a result of this statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn, Mr. Registrar, to 1D12-0084.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D62, marked for identification, Your Honour Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D62 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, this is an internal memo of the 7th of August from Mr. Stoltenberg to the Secretary General at the time. It's dated the 7th August, but the subject discusses a meeting with the Croatian foreign minister, Granic, in Geneva on 6 August, 1995. And the participants in the meeting, as you can tell from the first paragraph, were Mr. Stoltenberg, himself; the Spanish minister, Solana; EU foreign affairs commissioners, van den Broek; and Mr. Bildt?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, Mr. Registrar, to the paragraph starting with foreign minister Solana's rebuke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says that: "In their discussions with the Croatian foreign minister," it says, "Foreign minister Solana crisply reiterated the EU position deprecating Croatia's military actions, even as it was engaged in talks, condemned the shelling of civilian areas in Knin, expressed concern over the humanitarian situation, protested about the treatment of UN troops, and handed over a formal protest from Denmark about the treatment of its troops."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go on to the next section, Mr. Registrar, and that first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Granic was pressed to explain the shelling of civilian areas in Knin and was told in no uncertain terms that that involved war crimes, a matter falling within the province of the International Tribunal in The Hague. Would the Croatian government cooperate with the Tribunal in investigating the attacks on civilians? He did not answer directly, but said that there had been three military barracks in Knin and that most of the civilians had already fled the city before it was shelled. He was told that his explanation did not stand up to the known facts." From this document, and from your presence and subsequent role on the 7th of August, I'd just like to ask you if you recall, before entering Knin, that there was an expectation upon your arrival in Knin that civilian areas in Knin had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whether there was an expectation, I'm not sure I'd go that far, but I certainly considered that a possibility and that was one of the things we wanted to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were travelling with Mr. Akashi, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, on the 7th of August, that at the highest political levels in the International Community, claims were being made that the shelling of Knin was a war crime that would be investigated -- that may be investigated by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that specific fact, but I know that there were concerns raised at a high level and by the highest level officials about the conduct of the military operation; and that, for example, was one reason why I had such an interest in looking at the hospital, because there had been concern expressed that the hospital may have been targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the source of the information that the hospital had been targeted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was UN personnel on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the ground where?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Any specific UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Prior to your trip to Knin with Mr. Akashi, do you know of anyone who had independently gone into Knin to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fairly sure that our visit with Akashi was the first visit by international observers, but I'm not 100 per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So when this international delegation told Croatian Foreign Minister Granic that his explanation did not stand up to the known facts, as far as you know, the known facts are from the UN peacekeepers in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any and all UN personnel who were in Knin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Knin on the 7th, is it fair to say that you were surprised by the lack of damage to the town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised that there was less damage than I expected, yes. There certainly was damage, but it did not seem to be extensive in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, you indicated just now that you were specifically interested in the issue of whether the hospital had been shelled; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you went to the hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what did you conclude after your trip to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There did not appear to be significant damage there. I think there was evidence of at least one shell explosion that had not caused significant damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you advised at any point in the day that there was an RSK tank parked in front of that hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And who advised you of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a nurse at the hospital who told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically what she told you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there was a tank that had been positioned near the hospital that was firing outwards at the incoming Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would that have been on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. I'm not sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In this delegation to Knin, you travelled with Mr. Akashi and, forgive me if I mispronounce his name, Mr. Hubert Wieland?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Also in your delegation were journalists; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Journalists from the BBC?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Journalists from Croatian TV?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect so. There were quite a number of journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And upon your arrival, were you briefed by General Forand?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you briefed by anyone else? Let me be more specific. Were you briefed any anyone else from UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so much. The attention that day was, of course, focused on Mr. Akashi, and he was the one who spoke with individuals we met. Certainly, General Forand was concerned with speaking with Mr. Akashi and not with me. I was just a mid-level UN official in his delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you two video clips from that day and see if you recall the statements. These are reports from journalists who were with you on that trip to Knin, and I'd like to see if you recall what the journalist here is reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, are transcripts given to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we do, as usual. I don't know what the speed of speech will be there, but I'll follow the French translation whether they can keep up. Of course, first of all, you have given a number not yet to Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D63, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us would video transcripts in the different languages would all be under that same number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar will check in the system how it's uploaded. Meanwhile, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "But what is clear is that the Croatians are in control." "Well, very much so, yes. Their flags are flying everywhere in this town, which only 48 hours ago the Krajina Serbs regarded as their capital. Now it's totally under the control of the Croatians. The UN say that, as far as they can tell, the Croatians have been behaving with discipline and in a correct fashion."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could show the second clip then, this is from the Croatian TV report of that same trip to Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is, Mr. Registrar, 1D12-0092.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes D64, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Foreign military observers are credited in the Republic of Croatia have arrived in Knin today. Military officers from the U.S., Japan, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Poland, Slovakia, Great Britain, France, and Turkey were interested in the current situation in the liberated Croatian city of Knin. "They were first greeted at the UNCRO barracks in Knin by a Canadian officer of by the name of Tymchuk, who informed them that it was peaceful in Knin. He briefly commented on what he describes as a surprising entry by the Croatian army into Knin. Tymchuk said there was no major fighting, nor were any breaches of human rights. "Approximately, 700 Serb civilians took refuge in the UNCRO barracks where they are located now, and the Croatian authorities are attempting to ensure them sufficient food and medicine. The military envoys then visited the Knin hospital where they came across approximately 20 patients, some of which were wounded members of the Krajina paramilitary. "The head of the hospital, Dr. Ante Viskovic, briefed them on the current situation within the hospital and stressed that every doctor is bound by an oath, obligating him to treat all patients regardless of religious or national affiliation, or whether they are not civilians or members of the army. The senior military officials proceeded to visit the Knin fortress after which they continued on to visit Drnis."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, you were also there on the 7th of August. Do you recall UN personnel saying something to the effect that Croatian forces were behaving professionally and in a correct manner?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a sense at that time in Knin that they were doing so. I should point out that we got information from some of those 700 displaced persons which filled in the picture, so to speak; but on that first day, the situation seemed relatively stable and under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The 700 people were located in the UN compound; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the UN personnel in Knin would have had access to those same 700 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there was any attempt at all to get information or testimony from those individuals about what they had experienced. That was one of the reasons we went to Knin on the 7th. As far as I know, for example, the Canadian soldiers did not discuss with those 700 individuals or any of them what they had seen in the previous few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But the Canadian soldiers would not have had to interview one of the persons in the compound in order to say -- see massive fires going on, for example; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well that's true. I'm -- I would disagree with what Major Tymchuk is quoted as saying there, with respect to there being no human rights violations; but the violations did not relate, as far as I know, to extensively shelling of civilian areas. They were -- they took other forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In terms of your ability to move around town on the 7th, were you able to travel through the town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. On the 7th, we were just getting organised, and so our only movement within the town was as part of Mr. Akashi's delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in your visit to the hospital, did you find any signs of violations to the rights of the patients in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you find that, in fact, the Croatian government had allowed Serb staff that had been there from before the 4th of August to remain if they wished to remain in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you find in your trip to Knin that some patients had been evacuated from the hospital during the operation and taken to the UNCRO camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in the UNCRO camp on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I ended up spending the night there and quite a few nights afterwards. So I think we arrived there, it was probably mid-afternoon or so, and we didn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you told that there was a wing of the camp where 35 people were being given medical treatment because they had been removed from the hospital during the operation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, you were kind enough to meet with investigators of the Gotovina Defence earlier this year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: During the course of that interview, did you say that, from what you know, the exodus of Serbs from the Krajina was "rather remarkably organised"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I said that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you compare it to the exodus of Serbs from Kosovo years later?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have done so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is the comparison, then, if any, between the exodus of the Serbs from Krajina and the exodus of Serbs from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say "organised," I meant that perhaps "orderly" is a better word, in the sense that people were moving in one group along one road toward an evident shared destination. There didn't seem to be, you know, mass chaos and people running in different directions. Instead, there was a convoy that was moving out of the region, and that was also what we saw in Kosovo, that people evidently had considered this possibility of some sort of military operation, and when it happened they had likely already planned where to go and what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm conscious, Your Honour, of the need to take a break, so I'm just going to finish this area in one or two minutes and then we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that, Mr. Flynn, given your experience in the former Yugoslavia, were there examples of flight that was not organised or - let me quote you accurately, "orderly" - that was not orderly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In my experience, not a great deal; but, for example, I know -- well, during the beginning of the conflict, the information I had was that people leaving a certain zone did not do so in an orderly manner. For example, in any of the former sectors, I'm sure that - I mean, I know that - evacuations did not take place in this particular way. But, of course, in 1995, the war had been a fact for several years; and in this particular case, there was -- there were rumours that the Croatian military would be attacking, and that also happened in Kosovo, of course. So it was rather remarkable; and, certainly, the reality that when these operations happened, the evacuations were quite orderly, in the sense that everyone was moving together in one convoy, in one direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I have for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. We'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00, but not until I've asked the following question. D63 and D64, two videos you've just shown, English transcripts are uploaded. Of course we, always have the language of the accused as well. Do you have any translation for those so that the accused have access to it, because all the words are spoken in English so they can't look directly at the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We will provide one. The second video was in Croatian, so I assume they were able to hear that one. The first video we'll provide a B/C/S translation of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we leave a decision on admission for the time being. It may well be that the Prosecution has no problem of just having an English version; but, of course, the Chamber has to look at the public character of these proceedings as well. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Misetic, I do understand that a new translation replaces the old D31 translation, just for the parties to know. During the break, the Chamber gave some thought to very large documents, such as the 234 pages of the police log. As matters stand now, we leave it as it is. It could be that other pages, but many other pages, perhaps a few other pages, will become relevant in the future. Perhaps, the totality might gain some relevance. So, therefore, for the time, we leave it as it is. But it could be that if it's just our focus on a few incidents, that we might not need all these pages and we perhaps could deal with the cover page. At the same time, there might be authenticity issues as such were concerned. We will consider that and the parties are also invited to consider to what extent we need huge documents in their entirety or whether we can deal with selected portions, given sufficient context not to be misled by only that portion. For the time being, we leave it as it is, but it takes an enormous effort to have things printed out, if need be, to have materials summarised for us, if need be. So, therefore, the parties are invited to clearly look at what is relevant and what we might be able to do without. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, do you have a copy of your statement in front of you, statements, I should say?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On page 13 --
