utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of my first statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. My number 34, which is the last sentence on that page, says -- do you see that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Well, let's say, starting about the 14th or 15th of August, there was a noticeable increase in the number of burnings of houses that was taking place." The line goes on to page 14, line 1.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that still your recollection today, that the burnings started to increase around the 14th or 15th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. Because when I reviewed my notes, I saw that it was really around the 10th or 11th that we started to see quite a number of burnings south of Knin. But on the 13th, we took the drive to Benkovac, and that was when the previous number seemed way too low and it became apparent that there were an increasing number. So I would say the 14th or 15th is maybe a little -- a day or two late to refer to a notable increase in the number of burnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a preliminary question: When did you leave Sector South?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about the 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. On the next page of your statement, starting at line 3, you say: "At that time, well after hostilities had ceased, I would say that the burning was reaching its peak around maybe the 15th or 20th of August."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "At that time, it was an every day occurrence to see quite a number of fires that had been set in different locations. The burning started to wind down toward the end of the month; but, in fact, even into the first couple of weeks of September, it was November to find a burning structure in one place or another." Is it still your testimony today that the burnings reached their peak sometime around the 15th or 20th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so with respect to the entire area. What we saw really toward the end of August and in early September was that more specific areas were targeted. So, for example, I think it was on the 30th of August, I was on a team that travelled to Obrovac; and in the Obrovac area, we saw something like 15 houses that were burning that day. So, of course, the peak for Obrovac then would have been that day. But in terms of the overall sector and the overall daily number of burnings, it was probably around the 20th of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On page 17, line number 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One clarifying question. Mr. Flynn, you talk about the 14th, 15th, might have been a bit early; 11, 12, or on from the 10th. I have to carefully look now. Now, you started touring, as far as I understand, and perhaps in the beginning even limited, on the 9th of August. What was your point of reference in saying that it increased that much where you had not ample opportunity to observe personally at any earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was getting information from other UN observers, of course, in the field, the military observers and others; and it was around about the 14th or 15th that the high number of fires in the Benkovac valley was known to me. So I was basing and I am basing my assessment on, not only my own personal observations, but what I learned from others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apart from more fires, it could also be more reports of fires, to some extent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Flynn, if we could go to page 22, if we could deal with that first, line 29.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were asked to give an estimate of the houses destroyed, and your answer is: "When I mentioned the estimate of 500 houses destroyed, I'm referring to houses that were destroyed in the couple of weeks or two or three weeks after Operation Storm."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand the number is not intended to be a precise figure, but is that the general number of homes you recall during the month of August that had been burned?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's my own estimate, and I think I said somewhere else, I have always tended to be conservative in these estimates because I'm conscious that, by exaggerating, I would affect my own and others' credibility. But when I gave this statement of 500, that seemed to me an entirely realistic and, if anything, conservative estimate of the number of buildings that had been destroyed by the end of the third week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, your -- the end of the third week of --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would put us around the 28th or 29th of --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, roughly, the end of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At some point, your HRAT teams had nightly meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As part of those nightly meetings, did representatives of the UNMOs, the UNMOs, attend the meetings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone specifically from UNMO who would attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I refer to my notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm having trouble locating that. All right. I remember Colonel Sethsun [phoen] being quite involved in these meetings, and also Colonel Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an UNMO by the name of Anttila?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How about an UNMO named Mogulin [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did the UNMOs ever appear at an HRAT evening meeting and tell you that they had counted, let's say, 11.000 burned houses?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That number would have been something that you would have remembered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did they ever come back and say 16.000 houses?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the UNMOs were conducting a survey, and I know that their numbers were high. Again, as I say, when I refer to my own estimate, my extent is to be on the conservative side. I don't recall, though, any discussions with regard to those numbers while I was there, those kinds of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's discuss, then, what you would discuss at an HRAT meeting at which UNMOs are present; and if though counted 11.000 homes, would that not be something that would be discussed at an evening meeting of HRAT?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us, at least through your time, which is, I believe, you said the 16th of September, no UNMO came to a meeting and said, We've counted 11.000 burned houses?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only recall, and I only reported on, the sightings that had been made that day; and, yeah, I don't recall that we discussed any information like you've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said, in terms of how you arrived at your number of 500, you wanted to be conservative and you did not wish to exaggerate. In your experiences in Sector South, were there any elements of HRAT that you believe may have been prone to exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The report that you refer to by UNMOs -- or the survey, I should say, that was being prepared, was that being prepared for HRAT?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at least not when I was there. I've seen that survey subsequently, but it was an exercise in which I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If they started doing the counting while you were still in the field, and if it was to be someone from HRAT, would they have advised you that they were doing such a survey under the auspices of HRAT?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a little bit of a gap between what the HRATs did and what the UNMOs did. The UNMOs, the military observers, I would say, stuck fairly close to their own terms of reference. They participated in the HRATs, but not really as full-fledged human rights monitors, let's say. They had their own responsibilities, and they had their own method of reporting. So I think, in a way, they would have favoured their own reporting lines and reporting methods, and their involvement in the HRATs was not as sustained as their implementation of their own mandated activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Their mandated activities, as far as you know, would have been what is the Saranic/Akashi agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so, but I'm not recalling all the terms of that agreement off the top of my head. But the UNMO's primary responsibility, of course, was monitoring military activities, and they travelled more extensively than we did on their own. I would say there was a certain reluctance on the part of many of the UNMOs to share all of their information liberally with others, including a Human Rights Action Team. I think they felt -- the majority of them felt that they had really a separate mandate; and, as I say, their involvement in the Human Rights Action Teams was, in a way, rather informal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could turn back now to page 17 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, would you allow me. You're referring to page 22, where it reads, "When I mentioned that estimate of 500 houses," could you assist me in finding exactly where these 500 houses were mentioned before? Yes, I see it on line 29, "but when I mentioned that estimate of 500 houses," seems to refer to an earlier mentioning of the 500 houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I seem to recall that there wasn't a previous mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There wasn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, I was trying to understand exactly, on the basis of your earlier mentioning these 500 houses, to find out exactly what was the basis of your estimate. Did you just gain an impression when you were touring, or did you do some systematic approach? I mean, could it be, let's just assume, that you visited 50 villages and that you may have missed another 60 villages? I am asking how systematic the investigation, or at least the collection of data, which was at the basis of this conservative estimate of 500 houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to my own activities, I have to say that I did not undertake a systematic effort to count the number of burned buildings, and so this estimate is a personal estimate. I was one individual, the only representative of the Centre For Human Rights there; and I did not, in fact, engage in an effort to systematically count the number of burned buildings. This was actually something for which UNMOs would have been much better suited, since they had several vehicles on a daily basis all over the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also because you referred to there was kind of project by the UNMOs to -- I don't know exactly what you said. Perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A survey, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a survey. So it was an impression which you gained, during that period, not on the basis of a systematic research and systematic counting or a systematic visiting of all of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just, before he answers the question, I found the earlier reference. It is page 21, and it starts at line 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I was mistaken. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it doesn't appear in numbers, that's the difference. I see that and let me then read it again. It says, "at least," yes. Yes. Thank you. It doesn't give much information about the method used. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Flynn. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the witness respond to the question from the Bench, the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's, more or less -- Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At line 53 -- page 53, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question which was, more or less, summarizing what I understood your answer was. So it was an impression which you gained during that period, not on the basis of a systematic research and systematic counting or a systematic visiting of all of the villages. That was my question, whether I well understood your testimony in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I may have been aware that the UNMOs were engaging or about to engage in this systematic counting exercise, but I really don't recall that and I didn't get the results, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason, Mr. Flynn, why UNMOs would count 11.000 burned houses and then not advise the evening HRAT meeting of that number?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that question, Mr. President. The question presupposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Speculation. Well, I think, Mr. Misetic, that the matter has been dealt with already when you talk about these meetings, where you said this would have been discussed. The witness said he didn't remember that number, but he did remember that they had larger numbers. So now to further speculate on reasons, unless there is any specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, if we could get an understanding of the nature of the HRATs, because it's my understanding that the UNMOs were, in fact, one of the components of HRAT and under the Saranic/Akashi, it specifically says: "UNCRO human rights elements plus UNMOs will be doing the human rights reporting." So I just think it's unusual that UNMO would not pass that number on, at least to his recollection, and I believe he's testified that he would have recalled a number of that size. And just to explore, given his experience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But he has answered most of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, earlier in your testimony, I believe on direct examination, you mentioned that on the 4th of September, you came across two soldiers whom you believe to have been members of the 4th Split Brigade sitting in a village where a house was on fire nearby; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two buildings, I think, were on fire nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to know at that time where the 4th Guards Brigade was actually deployed on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you see tanks in the vicinity of the village?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some kind of transportation, but I don't recall whether or not they were armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could it have been civilian transportation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Any military operation underway that you could determine?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our access to that area to the Plavno Valley had been restricted in the previous days because, apparently, there was some sort of a so-called clean-up operation against RSK fighters still in the hills, and so there may have been some greater military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: On that day, was there sounds of gunfire or other visible or audible evidence that there was a military operation taking place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just as a background question, I've been passed a note: Were there any areas in Sector South that UNMOs patrol that HRAT teams could not patrol?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were, mainly because -- in fact, I'm quite sure they were. We relied on UNMOs, to a large extent, on a question of land mines, and we were very wary of travelling on small dirt roads. I think the UNMOs had a greater capacity to assess the risk and to move into areas that we wouldn't have covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you think of any specific places that you were unable to gain access to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some areas that we were blocked from getting into at the end of August and early September, as I say, when there were these activities along the eastern side of the former sector at the border with Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But let me stop you there. Were you aware that there was armed conflict taking place in Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that Croatian forces were involved in the armed conflict there Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the area that you were's talking about, was that the access point through which Croatian army forces entered and exited Bosnia at?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was that your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. The witness has said that he doesn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even if you don't know, sometimes you can understand certain information in a way which does not establish full knowledge but, at the same time, give an impression. So, therefore, the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just didn't know of -- I had no knowledge as to whether or not the Croatian forces were actually entering Bosnia. I didn't know about that. But if I could answer your previous question, it occurs to me that the UNMOs, as part of their possibility, were supposed to monitor military activities of the parties; and, in that respect, they probably went a lot closer to areas where there might have been some military activity than certainly we would have, as part of the HRAT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question, more or less, was that when you received the information that you had no access, whether you in any way, in that information, that you perceived something which might give you a clue to not getting access because military activity aiming at participation in an armed conflict across the border was the reason why no access was given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that reason was given, particularly for lack of access to the road to Donji Lapac, which was more or less parallel and close to the border with Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this is now your reconstruction at this moment. At the time, was there, apart from, well, the type of restriction imposed, was there anything else at that moment which made you think, Well, that's because they might participate in armed conflict across the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was there anything else that made me think that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, for example, they said, Don't go there; it's too close to the Bosnian border or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the 12th of August, I was with General Forand as he drove up the road to Donji Lapac, and I saw the Croatian military firing into Bosnia. I knew that that was an area of conflict, certainly, and that road was not always accessible to us and the reason given was that there were military activities taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to that incident with people you believe may have been members of the 4th Guards Brigade. Did you report that incident to the Croatian Military Police.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we reported that, again, to General Cermak's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you report it to the commander of the 4th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a little confusion in preparing for this cross-examination; so, hopefully, you can clarify it for me. Who was the person who was, let's call it the chain of command of HRATs, the most senior person for HRATs in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you would report to whom?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported really to our office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Any specific person that you would report to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wieland was the head of our mission in Croatia; so, technically, I reported to Mr. Wieland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Wieland was part of what?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the representative of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in Croatia; and in terms of seniority, he was the senior human rights officer in Croatia and he was the head of our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was that office part of UNCRO?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had sort of an unusual arrangement. Obviously, we were all the working for the UN, but we were independent but we relied in large part on the logistical support of UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have an UNCRO ID?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did all members of HRATs have UNCRO ID?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could next turn to page 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you where, apart from having an UNCRO IDs, did you have your own IDs at all next to that or.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question again based on your experience in the former Yugoslavia. Destruction of religious sites, in your experience, was that a common trait in ethnic cleansing campaigns, if I can call it that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you have any opinion as to why religious sites would be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is symbolism and the emotional harm, if you will, that it would cause to those who use those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 32 of the statement, line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "One thing that was striking at this time, however, was that the Croatian authorities were apparently paying special attention to religious sites, to Serb religious sites, and revisited the church and monastery at Krka. There were dozens -- there were some dozen Croatian soldiers stationed there protecting the place, and they let us go in. They stayed with us. They didn't let us go up to the second floor. "They said that they had found a weapons cache up there and they couldn't be sure the area was safe, but the monastery basically seemed to be in good condition and the artefacts inside were being protected. So this measure of protection for a religious site was rather striking, particularly compared to the apparent lack of protection that Kistanje was getting."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to wait for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In this portion of your statement, I believe you're referring to one Serb religious site, the monastery at Krka; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about other Serb religious sites throughout Sector South, did you note whether there was destruction of Serbian religious sites in Sector South during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't include reference to that in my reports, and my recollection is I don't particularly recall that there was damage particularly to other Serb religious sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When we say "religious sites," we mean churches, monasteries. Is there anything else that you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although -- I mean, it's hard to say because some of the towns had quite a bit of destruction, and it could have been that a church had been burned down and I couldn't tell that it was a church or not. But I didn't note in particular the destruction of other Serb religious sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if I can raise it this way, if there was a systematic campaign to target Serb religious sites, would that have been something that would have made its way into one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could turn next to page 20, number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you discuss an incident that came to your attention on the 12th of August related to a pair of murders which took place in Knin.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "A patrol had been contacted by a local resident, a woman who was in Knin, and I went out on the call with a couple of other UN colleagues, including, I remember, Mr. Roberts."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "When we got to the scene, which was not far from the centre of Knin, the neighbour, a woman, told us she had reason to believe that there were some corpses in the house next to hers. We went into the house, and we found two dead bodies of older men. They were quite decomposed, and it appeared that they had been shot in the head where they were sitting. They were sitting in the living-room -- no, excuse me. One man was sitting in the living-room, and one was -- I'm trying to recall. I think one was on a bed in the bedroom." Then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could pull up, Mr. Registrar, 1D12-0113.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you while that's being pulled up, do you recall whether UN CIVPOL was also at this scene?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D65, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As you can see this is an UN CIVPOL report from the 25th of August, 1995, which is the date that you reference in your statement. Then towards the middle there, it says: "The two monitors visit the place and saw the two bodies on the first floor: One in the kitchen sitting in a chair, this was an old man; the other one on the floor in a room to the left close to the window. The window was opened and it," the word there is "science," but it should be "seems," "that the man tried to escape. Because of the long time, it was impossible to see how the two men died. CIVPOL monitors called for civilian policija, and a special team came to the spot and took care of the bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then we'll move to two other documents, Your Honour, with respect to this incident. These have already been admitted into evidence and are D7. These are autopsy reports on these two individuals. If Your Honour wishes, I believe we went through this in the examination of the first witness. If the Court wishes, I can show him the names and how they relate to the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If there's no objection, I would just rather go straight to the document to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first autopsy report, if you look at the third paragraph, Mr. Flynn, it says: "The only ante-mortem injury identified to the bone was a single fracture of the left 10th rib laterally, without any special characteristics whatsoever. Its significance was uncertain. In the absence of any soft tissues and any pathology or significant trauma, the cause of death remained undetermined. No other significant findings were made."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could show D8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, second sentence: "There were no fresh injuries of ante-mortem or peri-mortem nature." Then the fourth paragraph: "The cause of death is unascertained anatomically."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then if we could go back to the first document -- D65, marked for identification. That is the CIVPOL report from that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your statement, at line 22: "They were quite decomposed, and it appeared that they had been shot in the head where they were sitting."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 20, line 22.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you see a bullet wound to the head on these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw what I believed to be a bullet wound in the head of the individual who was seated; but, of course, I'm not a pathologist, so I couldn't swear that that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you saw a bullet wound to the head, were you discussing the incident with the UN CIVPOL team that was there as well?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where in the head did you see the bullet wound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you were --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there might be a photograph of this individual, but I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you were discussing this, do you have any explanation for why the UN CIVPOL report would say, "Because of the long time, it was impossible to see how the two men died."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no explanation. I'm not sure why they would say that, but I would tend to credit the views of police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Meaning UN CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So as between your account and UN CIVPOL's account, you would credit the UN CIVPOL account?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's a matter for the Trial Chamber, not to ask the witness to weigh one version against the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's his own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, I do agree with you, Ms. Mahindaratne, that it's the Trial Chamber that will have to decide. But if someone has made some observations, if they are put in a statement, and if that witness is then -- if it's then put to the witness that there are other observations, including autopsy reports, then it's not inappropriate to ask the witness that in view of all this material, how - and that's, of course, what the core of the question is - how certain the witness is that his observation which is of a technical nature is accurate. I understand that this witness now tells us that in view of what the others say, that he does not exclude for the possibility that it's inaccurate. That's how I understood the line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is no need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: However, there is another matter, Ms. Mahindaratne. Usually, if someone is shot in the head, it's my experience, although I'm not an expert in this field, that this usually leaves traces on the scalp. Usually, entry wounds and exit wounds are visible. I would not exclude for the possibility that you can shoot someone through the head, for example, through the eye, and then somewhere leaving. But that's not what you usually find. Where this witness says that there may have been photographs or that he even thinks that there were photographs made, in order to finally enable the Chamber to make the right determinations, apart from having this statement of this witness and his testimony today, and apart from having autopsy reports, and apart from having this police report, photographs might assist us in finally making such determination. So whether it would be in favour of or against you, I don know; so, therefore, I'm addressing both parties to see whether these photographs can be retrieved, so that the Chamber has an additional instrument to make the determinations it will have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, Mr. Kehoe advises me that we have, in fact, looked through the materials that have been produced to us, and there is no photograph that we know of that has been produced in the case thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, we can ask the witness. You said, "I think photos were made." Do you have any recollection of who would have made those photographs or who would usually do that under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think that Mr. Roberts may have. He often carried a camera with him, Alun Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that these might have been a kind of private photographs, not professionally taken but for personal purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't characterise it that way, necessarily; but he's, you know, a media officer for the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, perhaps in consultation with Mr. Misetic, but the Chamber would very much like to know whether, what the witness just told us, that Mr. Roberts might have such photographs, whether that is the case or not. I don't know, I take it that you will find a way in how to address Mr. Roberts to see whether this additional piece of information could become available for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I note that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, I'd like to turn next to the issue of reception centres. I'd like to show you a document and ask you if you agree with the findings in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The document, Mr. Registrar, 1D12-0016. If you could turn the page, please, the next page. Your Honour, it will take a moment. I believe this is a large exhibit, and I will have to find the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't seem that there's much conclusions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just keep flipping through the pages, Mr. Registrar, and I'll tell you when to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, there are 35 pages so it might take quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I have a copy here on my screen, Your Honour, so I'll find it faster. Page 3, Mr. Registrar, the first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a U.S. government report provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. It's dated 14 August 1995. The fifth line down in that first full paragraph, it reports: "Roughly 500 Serbs remain at the United Nations Headquarters compound in Knin. Another 250 are located in a camp run by Croatian police in a school. None of the Serbs who spoke with us complained of mistreatment by Croatian authorities, and GOC," which I believe is shorthand for government of Croatia, "civil authorities have taken great pains to demonstrate publicly their commitment to protect Serbs and Serb property. "Poloff observed, however, isolated attempts to intimidate and humiliate remaining Serbs. Many Serbs expressed fear of remaining in a Croatian state; although, several from small villages and the countryside said they did not intend to leave their land." Mr. Flynn, is it correct to say that the -- there was no evidence of mistreatment of Serbs in the school reception centre in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, there were no complaints of mistreatment there by those who were staying there for purposes of shelter. I think there was an issue later when persons accused of participation in the conflict were held in a slightly separate area as POWs, essentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you introduced this document, and you said that the witness would be invited to see whether he shared the conclusion of that document. The document does not draw the conclusion you later phrased, at least that there's no evidence of the document saying that there are no complaints. The experience in this Tribunal has learned that not always the fact that someone who remains in a place where it's still to be seen, whether he remains there voluntarily or not, that if he does not complain about the treatment, that not automatically means or could not be understood as clear evidence of no ill treatment. I would not have raised the issue if you would not have told the witness that you would ask him to join or not to join a conclusion. That is a conclusion now mixed up the observations in the report, and the conclusion you put to the witness are not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did any Serbs in the school complain to you about mistreatment during your visits to the school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness had already seen different, so he started his answer by saying, They did not complain. So I was commenting object your question. The witness understood apparently well what he read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Very good. Page 2 of that document from the middle to the bottom -- I'm sorry, paragraph 4 of the document, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "All remaining Serbs in Knin were in two locations: The United Nations compound or the GOC-controlled camp at the local school." Is that an accurate statement, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is dated August 9th, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's the 14th.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a few Serbs in Knin itself, but not very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The majority, though, were in one of the two camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "There were almost no military-aged men among them." Is that accurate, in terms of the people in the two camps, there were almost no military age men among them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So now we're talking about the military compound and the school?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so sure. I seem to recall that there were -- well, there were certainly military age men at the UN compound, and I think there were a small number at the school as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "The UN camp held about 500 Serbs. Most were sleeping outdoors under plastic, although some (particularly women with small children and the infirm) were sleeping in the basement of the UN building." Is that an accurate statement of the conditions in the UN camp around the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "UN officials say the refugees were receiving the same food as the UN troops: A very basic meal, two times a day. Potable water was scarce." Are those accurate statements?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so sure about that. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which part of the statement are you not sure about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if the refugees were getting two meals a day and I don't recall a problem with potable water, but there are others who would be far more knowledgeable about the actual living conditions of the refugees in the UN camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to page 5 of this exhibit, Mr. Registrar, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Conditions at the GOC-controlled camp were better, where about 250 Serbs were living in a school gymnasium. All had a roof over their heads, and most had mattresses." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "GOC officials had provided them with three meals a day and had trucked in sufficient water." Do you know if that statement is accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "As Poloff was visiting the camp, some of the Serbs were told that they were free to return to their homes." Do you know if Serbs in the school were being told that they could return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds correct. I think all Serbs at both facilities were being told that, if they wished and once they had obtained a propusnica, they could leave the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So they were detained there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on and says: "The camp administrator said that he believed that all the inhabitants would be released by August 15th." Did that happen that all the school inhabitants left on August 15th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How long did they stay in the school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure of the fluctuation of the population there. My recollection is that there were always at least some inhabitants at the school; and a couple of weeks later, of course, we were interested in moving some of the people at the UN camp into the school because of the overcrowding at the UN camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The last sentence says: "A UN human rights monitor told Poloff that he had received reports that 40 military age men had been taken from the camp on August 10 to Zadar for additional processing." Do you believe you may be the human rights monitor referred to there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I may well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now show another video. Sorry, Your Honour. I'm advised that I need to ask for a number for this document that we're looking at, and to ask whether it can be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then first see what it is because we -- it seems to be a U.S. report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will propose that we mark it for identification, and then I will just submit the documents, the three or four pages of documents that we've looked at today, because as you are aware, I believe there's 34 pages all told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't need the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that you select the pages and the cover letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which seems to indicate what we find there, and that a section you have used, and we give that one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be perhaps easier for Mr. Registrar, rather than to work with three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That becomes Exhibit D66, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, is there already an opinion about --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D66 is admitted into evidence on the basis of the selection to be made by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic, I think you were about to give a number to Mr. Registrar for the video to be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, I'm about to show you a portion. This is dated 9 August 1995. It is a video of your visit to the school. It's a portion, I believe, of your visit to the school. I'd just like you to take a look at it, and I'll ask you some questions about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, transcripts are provided to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Do you know how many people are located here? "They are from all over, Benkovac, Subrovac [phoen], Drnis, Knin, mostly from Knin, and the surrounding villages. Some of are them are from Gobovic [phoen], as well. You take a look at the list. It is very precise. Basically, they come from all over to register themselves and to get food, to report themselves. "The documents they can get only here, and the documents can only be obtained here? "Yes, here, and probably I'm not sure whether issuing any at the UN camp. Yes, they were over there and over there. "How long will it take the time to make one pass for these people? What is the time? "For a pass, this depends; but generally in a very short period of time. If somebody came this morning, he will get a pass this afternoon. "Is anyone saying they are afraid to leave this place? Is anyone afraid to leave from here? "No, no. They can't wait to get to their homes. They have cows, live stock. They are hardly waiting to go to their homes because they have cattle: "Have you been interviewing them? Are you interviewing them? Did you go and talk to them? "We were here last night, and there were about 40 men here. "Have they left? "They heard that 40 men arrived here last night. "Have they already left? "Those were the POWs. This is something different. This is not the same case. These are people who surrendered or who were captured with weapons and who were brought in and arrested by the military police. Those are the people who are detained by the military police with weapons. They will also probably go now to Sibenik or Zadar. All of them are having their pictures taken all of their information is being obtained. "Chief, do any of the people hearsay they want to go to Bosnia or they want to go to Serbia? Did anyone say they'd like to go to Bosnia, Serbia: "We didn't hear of this. The people only want to go home. The livestock is waiting to be tended to."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, does that video accurately record at least a portion of your trip to the school on the 9th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the information you had obtained about 40 men having been taken from the school, did you see that discussion there on the video?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you note that there was a difference between what the police chief had said about what happened to the men and how it was translated back to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll replay the portion of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a little before that, before that. Okay. Play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "They were about 40 men here. Have they left?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They heard that 40 men arrived here last night. Have they already left? "They were prisoners of war. This is something different. It is not the same case. Those were people who had surrendered and who were captured or who were captured with weapons and who were brought in and arrested by the military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what the police chief says, and now this is what you were told by the translator.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. So there is a difference in the two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe what you think the difference is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you back up just one more time, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Those are people who were brought in by the military police who had surrendered or were captured with weapons."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the original statement was more detailed. It referred to people who had surrendered, others who had been detained by military police. So there was more information in the original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There could have been confusion that, as opposed to people being arrested by military police with weapons, it was that people with weapons had been arrested by military police. There may be a fine distinction.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might be a confusion there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm advised I need to ask for a number for the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is Exhibit D67, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just inquire -- I beg your pardon. May I just inquire if the Defence is tendering only that clip or whether there is a full footage of the visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the entire. It's all raw footage that we have. This section is in its entirety the section that relates to Mr. Flynn. I have nothing else on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On that visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me just try to remember. Was everything that was said in English audible translated into B/C/S? I'm just considering whether we have a full record also in B/C/S of what we have here. The transcript is just English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a relatively short one, relatively short footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I would prefer to have B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, D67, we are waiting for a B/C/S translation before we finally decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One follow-up question: Mr. Flynn, do you recognise the chief by name in that video? Have you seen him in other places?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't recognise him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are done with the persons present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, I saw, from the right-hand side, I saw a person in a more blueish uniform with apparently an insignia on the shoulder, "Policija," was that the chief of the camp or the chief of this institution at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The individual who was answering my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he had that responsibility, Your Honour, but he certainly had some responsibility for management of the camp. He may have been a spokesperson and not the senior person there. I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next to him was someone standing in a brownish-green camouflage uniform, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was a UN military observer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A UN military observer, yes. I was just trying to find out who was who. Then you put one question to your interlocutor, asking whether they had any fear to go out, to leave, or whatever. Did you put questions about fear also to those who were staying in this, in that facility, because it struck me a bit that if a facility is organized by these -- there seems to be someone in charge who is a police officer; then to ask to that police officer whether the other people remaining there, whether they had any fear to do this or that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I certainly would have asked the refugees themselves, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interested in the police officer's impression, but I certainly would have gone to the primary source for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was the result of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection was that, at that point, most people wanted to get out of the school and, as the officer said, back to their farms. I think they were concerned that their farms were being untended at that point. Now, I wouldn't uniformly say that applied to everyone, but particularly -- well, I'm sure that most of the people wanted to get back to their farms at that point. This was only the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will just ask a few follow-up questions to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, would it be fair to say that because the people who were living in Sector South prior to the 4th of August, 1995, were living under the so-called government of the RSK, that the overwhelming majority of them did not have proper Croatian documentation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there was an issue regarding that; and yes, of course, Croatia had only come into existence a few years before. So, yes, many of those people, probably most of them, did not have Croatian documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How, in your experience that you were there, how could the Croatian authorities determine which of the people that were still there had a lawful right to be on that territory and which had come in from, let's say, Bosnia, Serbia, or some other part of the former Yugoslavia and was not a, if I can phrase it this way, a lawful resident of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to recall that there was some interest in locating records that had been maintained prior to the conflict and that would have indicated who had resided there previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the process of trying to match the individual with the records, where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not sure. That's something the Croatian authorities were handling, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did it take place in the school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have, but I think that would have been too early, really. I think, at that point, there was an effort made to identify if the persons had been actively involved in the conflict, and who could be given a propusnica to simply move around. I think, at that point, freedom of movement was the issue and not really lawful residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll turn to my final topic, Mr. Flynn. I noted in the transcript the your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I refer now to the transcript of your testimony at page 1107, lines 17 to 25, page 1108, line 1. You said: "In speaking for myself, I didn't usually press General Cermak on the question of who he was in contact with in Zagreb. From my point of view, my concern was the local security situation and providing due notice to the General."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You never provided due notice to General Gotovina of the security situation in Sector South, did you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I ever spoke directly with General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you write him a letter to put him on due notice of the security situation in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a relatively mid-level UN official, and I did not consider that it was for me to independently contact General Gotovina. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you were independently contact General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think the witness hadn't completed when counsel interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first verify. Had you completed your answer when Mr. Misetic put the next question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Just one more phrase, Your Honour, which is that I understood all along, as I think I've made clear, that General Cermak was a responsible authority in the region and that he was the appropriate person to communicate with, with regard to concerns that we had. I consider that it was adequate to contact General Cermak on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you specifically with respect to you, and you had used the phrase "due notice ," so just to be clear for the record, and it's my last question: You, personally, did not provide due notice to General Gotovina of the security situation in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're asking me a legal question. I don't know. Would it be due notice if I informed another senior military official? I'm really not sure of that. But I didn't. I don't believe I ever spoke personally with General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions of the.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I think we should take a break now. Ms. Mahindaratne, if you could inform us on how much time you would approximately need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe about 40 minutes to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Forty to 45 minutes. We'll have a break until 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're offering to could the re-examination as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have to correct the record and that's why I am on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You had asked for the photos. I had indicated that we do not have them. As it turns out, during the break, I discovered that we do have the photos, and they are on the Prosecution 65 ter list. We received them sometime in February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I earlier expressed that - I don't know whether they are of any assistance - but if you have looked at it and if could give any clue as to better understand whether this person had visible signs of head injury or even a shot wound, then, of course, the Chamber would like to see it. If there's nothing on it, but a clear picture of the head, of course, the Chamber would also like to see that. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have the photographs here. Can I just send it to you or would you prefer me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we first ask the usher to just briefly show them to us, so that we can see whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could even call it up on the screens, Mr. President. It's 65 ter 159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could do that and then see whether it's of any use. The subject seems to be relevant, but not always a picture gives relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 5 to 6, there are two photographs, if you go to page 5 first. Mr. President, do you wish me to inquire from the witness if he recognises this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The picture, yes, perhaps that would be good. You see it now on the screen, Mr. Flynn. Is this what you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is another picture on the next page, Mr. President. This is one body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So these are pictures of the same individual, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These two photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, you could look at it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I see the other photograph? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you go to the top photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I could see the first photograph then, I think that was the one that I referred to as having been shot in the head. I don't know. I would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the next. Let me just try to understand what I see. Could we move up again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say this doesn't really square with my memory of this incident and the placement, so to speak, of the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go further down again. Please up again. I'd like to have the hard copies for a better comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber took some time, first of all, to find out about these two photographs, where apparently the person portrayed, the deceased person portrayed, is not in the same position on the two photographs. It seems that the body has been moved, which, if you carefully compare them, it looks as if -- or at least that the photograph is taken from a different angle. The one is not a -- it could be that the body has not been moved, but the photograph has been taken from different angles. I'd like to hear from the parties whether they consider it useful. May I take it that the photograph which is now on our screen, that is 0606-7513, that that is the body of which we saw an autopsy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, these two individuals are the two individuals that we previously put in autopsies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, both Ilija Vitojevic and Milan. I think we have exhibit numbers. They were Exhibit D7 which is Ilija, and D8 is Milan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be good to have them in evidence, so that they have some other material which may assist us and further consider whether the observations made by the police officer, by this witness, or by the autopsies are reliable. Then both of them, would you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would you tender them?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that then would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P52, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we take them together, that might be practical. No objection. Then P52 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Mahindaratne, of course, there might be some questions from the Chamber as well. Yesterday, you said you hardly would have anything; so, therefore, the 40 minute came as a bit of a surprise. Could you try to finish in until 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number D29, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, yesterday, you were questioned on behalf of Mr. Cermak on the basis that your conclusions or your impressions about Mr. Cermak's authority were inaccurate, and you were shown a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: One of the documents that was shown to you, in fact, supporting that -- or the Defence position was that this document supports that suggestion is this memo from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could we please move on to page 2, please. Now, in paragraph 4, if you could focus on that paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's reported that as follows, and this is Mr. Akashi writing: "My meeting with General Cermak went very well. He pledged to respect fully the agreement signed by Mr. Saranic and myself yesterday, copies of which I shared in English and Serbo-Croat. "He reiterated on several occasions that his forces would comply, not only with the agreement, but also with international standards for human rights, as well as the laws of war." Then further down, about the 10th or the 11th line, it says -- it further goes on to say: "Cermak assured me that the population had nothing at all to fear from his forces, and asked that I assist in conveying this message to the people." There's also reference to Mr. Cermak's assurances about safe passage to be provided to the population. Now are these assurances and statements provided by Mr. Cermak consistent with the suggestion put to you by the defence or are they consistent with the impressions you formed about Mr. Cermak's authority, in that are these the type of statements Mr. Cermak made to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. General Cermak addressed these kinds of issues; and it appears to me by looking at this document, which I had not seen before, that Mr. Akashi also assigned to General Cermak a certain amount of authority that is rather significant with regard to the forces there. I considered that the description that was discussed yesterday, I think, of the responsibilities of a garrison commander were not really consistent with what I understood General Cermak to be exercising, but that's also why I said I wasn't 100 per cent sure of his entire responsibility. It was clear to me that he had a greater responsibility than some of these issues such as, I don't know, securing logistical conditions or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While we are still on that document, I'm going to put to you a question on behalf of Mr. Gotovina. On paragraph 3, in paragraph 3, the same page, the document records that: "The hospital was large and in generally good condition, having been hit by only one artillery round." Now, in one of your reports, too, you record the Knin hospital having been hit by one artillery round; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have document D31, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you were shown Mr. Cermak's letter of appointment; and today, in fact, I have an accurate English translation of that document, which records Mr. Cermak being appointed as commander of the Knin garrison, and not the Knin garrison headquarters as it was first recorded in the previous draft translation. Do you note the document there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you note that Mr. Cermak's rank, as indicated here, is Colonel-General?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Cermak was -- had a rank of General. You know, in fact, in reports, you refer to him as General Cermak in your dealings.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding was that he had the rank of General.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note that Mr. Cermak's predecessor, the former Knin garrison commander, was a Major, Major Marko Gojevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note that Mr. Cermak's appointment comes directly from the president, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to waste court time, but do you recall the Defence showing you a document, yesterday, and I'm referring to D32, where it was recorded that garrison commanders were appointed by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In that context, do you see this appointment as being within the former structure as discussed by Mr. Kay yesterday, or do you see a difference here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There seems to be a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you elaborate what you mean?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that the General was appointed by the President of the Republic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To a position --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as the commander of the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you were also questioned about your reference to Mr. Cermak as military governor; and you, in fact, testified that Mr. Cermak was introduced to you as military governor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who introduced Mr. Cermak to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- frankly, the indication was probably given to us prior to our arrival even in Knin, and I met General Cermak for the first time when he visited the UN compound on the 8th of August. I'm afraid I can't say who introduced him, so to speak, but, I mean, it was made evident that he had a certain rank. But I can't say for sure where the term "military governor" came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you were questioned yesterday further about Mr. Cermak's authority over civilian police?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you were particularly -- it was suggested to you that when you used the term "order," that Mr. Cermak ordered the civilian police, that you were then perhaps referring to Mr. Cermak, using the term, "I will 'speak' to the civilian police ." And in relation to this, I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up document 2736, and that, Mr. President, was on the list sent to us by the Defence as being one of the exhibits they intended to use, but did not use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We need a number for that, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While that is being done --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honours, that becomes P53, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't think we still have it on the screen. It's 2736.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
