utterances.text: You recall, in examination in chief, I questioned you about a particular meeting at which Mr. Cermak informed you that he would order the Knin chief of police for -- to send reinforcement, and I asked you the question whether you heard the term "order" being used by Mr. Cermak and you said so?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that correct? Did you hear him say, "I will order," or did you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it was translated to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if we could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if you want to have a Defence document on the screen, then the Defence has to release that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Actually, the 65 ter number is from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is from the Prosecution. Did you release that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it has been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it has been released, then, Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I just have a hard copy placed on the ELMO for the time being, so I don't waste court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can do that for the time being. Of course, the witness should remove his material from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have both the English and the B/C/S there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start from the English for the time being, and we'll leave the other on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is apparently a duplicate. There were several versions of this document. 866, I'm told on the Prosecution's 65 ter is where it will also be found. I see Mr. Monkhouse nodding his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may be just be permitted to read the document into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that we get it now on our screen any how. So the electronics have won from the old techniques. Please proceed. Is this the document you had on your mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. This is not the document, Mr. President. It's a document number 0206-8325. This is a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm lost now with numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm told that there is a technical problem, Mr. President, and the wrong document is coming up. So I think it looks as if we will have to rely on hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it's a technical problem or a human failure is still to be seen, but let's -- the outcome of the match is that the traditional techniques have now won.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, do you note this document which is an order issued by Mr. Cermak to the Knin police, the Knin Military Police, the Knin police station. Do you note that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, in fact, it reads: "As of 8 August from 1500 hours, all UNCRO elements with clearly displayed insignia may move freely in the area of Knin and Drnis." This is an order issued by Mr. Cermak to the Knin Military Police and Knin Civilian Police with regard to freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the third paragraph reads: "This order takes effect immediately."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So do you read this as Mr. Cermak issuing orders to Knin Military Police and civilian police?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this document in evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P54, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P54. I take it, Ms. Mahindaratne, that this document, an order dated the 8th of August with the content, I should just put to the witness, will be uploaded into e-court, so that we have a record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion. I do understand that the hard copy that was put on the ELMO received already number P53. So this document, which we've seen in hard copy, dated the 8th of August, the order with immediate effect, is still P53. But the electronic version is to be uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I move to document number D35, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, you were shown this document. I think it's taking a moment for the English version to come up on the screen. Mr. Kay suggested to you in showing this document, and I'll use Mr. Kay's exact language about that this document: "The essential thrust of the whole of this order is that the military police are subordinated to the military police administration." On that suggestion, Mr. Kay showed this document to you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And he read out some paragraphs of this document. Let me read out a very pertinent paragraph. And if I could focus on paragraph 3, it reads that: "In accordance with Article 9 of the Rules, VP platoons," VP is a reference military police, "attached to the brigades are subordinated to the brigade commander, and through him to the commander of the military district Croatian navy, Croatian air force, and public security in performing daily military police tasks." Now, in reading that paragraph, what do you understand the subordination of the military police to be for the daily military police tasks, and I do appreciate you don't have a military background, but since the document was put to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would object. I think we've established this morning that taking this witness through Croatian military documents and asking him for an essentially a military or legal opinion on subordination may not be the most appropriate. We won't have re-direct on this but through other witness. Obviously, I just want to reserve our position on the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, the witness was asked to give his understanding with these kind of documents by Defence counsel, who introduced these documents; so, therefore, I allow Ms. Mahindaratne to put these questions, and it's on the record, your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say your reservations on the record. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne. You may answer the question, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding is that military police - and I can only reiterate what it says there - the military police attached to brigades are subordinated to the brigade commander and through him to the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's already in evidence, Mr. President. I will move on. May I have document D43, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you were shown -- while the document comes up, you were shown a document where 100 civilian protection conscripts were being sent, and it was suggested to you by Mr. Kay that these 100 men were being sent to police the area. Now, if you could focus --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't think I said police the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think the reference was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me the reference, then we can look it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's pages, from yesterday's transcript, Mr. President, 58 to 60. And while certainly Mr. Kay didn't use the word "police," the suggestion was clearly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we had a discussion about the use of a particular word. I remember Your Honour raising the point of different interpretations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said 58 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could read it here, it is a question on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY SAYS
utterances.text: "Yes. But on the face of this order, it seems that this assistant minister was ordering that rapidly and urgently that 100 conscripts go to the area." Answer: "That's what it says, yes." Question: "And, in fact, it was a concern of yours about the failure of the police to order more policemen to the area, and that's apparent from your statement." Clearly, the reference was that these were -- this was police reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well it does not literally say so. "Failure of the police to order more police to the area." Now, put your question. We have read what question was put to you yesterday. To that extent, Mr. Kay's words are now there accurately. Please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, on this issue, you raised a very pertinent question. You asked as to what rapid terrain clearance meant, and that was not properly explored. In paragraph 1 of this document, the reference is to "urgently mobilise 100 civilian protection conscripts from the area of Sinj." Now, from your understanding, and you working in human rights matters in conflict areas, what type of activity are members of civilian protection movements used for, policing or other type of humanitarian work such as collection of bodies, clearance of terrain, of debris, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that it relates more to the humanitarian situation of populations and to their humanitarian needs such as food, water, energy requirements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2, there is a reference: "The unit must report to Mr. Stanko Batur of the Knin police station." Now, do you know or have you heard of that name and a reference to him as being in charge of the sanitation and hygiene unit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds familiar, but I can't recall offhand what I knew his role to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two documents. I could lead into evidence just to give the Trial Chamber an accurate picture of this matter, but we could always lead that evidence later on. Would you prefer to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, in view of the time, and there is still a possibility that what the position of Mr. Batur is, perhaps the parties could even agree on that. Yes. It seems that there is some body language which raises high expectations in this respect. We have seen the same with documents Mr. Cermak being appointed, et cetera. These are matters which I would say in 80 per cent of the cases would be ready for agreement on. This is a decision by which he was appointed; the position of Mr. Batur was this or that. Of course, if there's any challenge to any of these matters, then, of course, the Chamber will hear the evidence about it. But these certainly are matters which should not take too much time in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do my speeches have to take much time in court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked today about collection centres. You visited the collection centre or the refugee centre in Knin school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there numbers of women, elderly, and children, displaced persons in that school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know how they got to that place? Did they come voluntarily or were they brought there by Croatian forces, perhaps the civilian police, or members of the military police? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe most, if not all, of those individuals were collected by Croatian authorities and brought there. They did not, as far as I knew, come on their own. In fact, people who would have come on their own typically went to the UN compound, because I think those people came of their own accord, and they came because of security concerns for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you ever offered an explanation by Mr. Cermak or any member of the Croatian authorities as to why people were taken to the school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, there was an interest in registering people; and in some cases, I think some people may have been removed from certain areas where it was expected there might be some kind of military activity. I'm afraid my recollection is not very clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was there a registration process at the Knin school where the persons were properly registered?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what happened to the majority of those people? Did they return to their villages, or were they transported out of the country?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think most of those people, at least in the first instance, returned to their homes. Now, there were a significant number of people who began showing up at the UN compound toward the end of August, and I don't know if that may have included some people who at one point had been in the school. But I think that the numbers of people at the school went down in the first couple of weeks, and I think that was mainly because many of those people did wish to at least try to go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, it was suggested to you, and you were questioned on the basis on behalf of Mr. Gotovina, that these people could leave the collection centre, and there was no detention involved. Now, was the situation outside the -- these camps or the collection centres conducive for people to return to their villages?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that evolved over time. I think people had had very different experiences, people who -- the people I spoke with in the UN compound who had come from the areas to the south of Knin which had seen the military or at least one part of Operation Storm directly, those people did not seem so keen to go back because I think of experiences that they had had. But for other individuals that were coming from other areas that really had not, until that point, seen any sort of fighting or threatening military activity, they were willing to try to go back, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you say that those -- there was some people, a segment of the number of people who were there, who were not so keen to go back "because I think of experiences that they had had." Now, could you elaborate on what exactly you are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that respect, I'm speaking of the information that we got from several witnesses about what I consider to be crimes committed against persons who were essentially fleeing the oncoming Croatian army. And, in some cases, according to the information we received, there were subject to threats; and, in some cases, saw people being shot on the spot. The -- there was a gap, so to speak, between the great majority of people who did leave the region in advance of the Croatian army, and I think some people who were furthest from the exit point. There were a number of people from the Drnis region who did not end up making it in time, I think, to the convoy; and their experiences were rather different from those who were at the head of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Flynn. That concludes the re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, in the reports that you compiled for the daily reports, specific ages are given to, or rather, in relation to the victims whose bodies were found in various places. How were these ages determined? I'm assuming that not every body or every victim had identification particulars on them.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was actually rather rare to find individuals with identification, as I recall. So most of the information regarding age came from neighbours, and some of that information may not have been totally accurate. I mean, for example, someone may have been identified as 60 years old, when they were 58 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, I have a few questions for you as well. In one of the documents, we saw that it was reported that -- I think it was Mr. Cermak who proposed joint patrols. I think it was -- I haven't got the source right here at this moment. Did they -- and I understood joint patrols to be UN/Croatian patrols; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in the early days, Your Honour? I remember -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think it was later. I think it was somewhere early September.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember if that was General Cermak's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there was a suggestion to have joint patrols early September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed, between the UN CIVPOL and the Croatian civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question is: Were there ever joint patrols? Was there just the proposal or a suggestion or was there ever joint patrols?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was rather fitful at the time I was there. I refer to this one instance in which it didn't work because of the fuel problems. As long as I was there, Your Honour, I don't remember there being a regular system of joint patrols. But, as I say, UN CIVPOL's method of operation throughout the entire former Yugoslavia, and for that matter in other UN operations, is typically to work directly with the local police. So I'm fairly sure that they were involved in joint patrols with the Croatian police toward the end of my stay there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the early stages.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if you would allow me one second to find a document. I apologise, but I have to look at this. You will remember D52, and what I was looking for was the exact date of D52, and it might be that that's a document which has no clear date. But if the parties could assist me, that would be appreciated; otherwise, I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was a letter that I think was back to front, and that page 6 is the cover letter for it, dated the 7th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I see that the first page of that document gives an unclear date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there, in D52, we saw a number of 91 persons on a list. You remember that list?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the dead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not only the dead. I think it were the persons that were in the school at that time.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You remember that list.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we heard a number of 250 in the school. Here we have a list of 91. Could you give us any impression on the development of the numbers, because you said that at the time they were supposedly be released, they did not -- the school was not empty after that. Could you give us a more general impression on how the numbers of people in that school developed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, the authorities actually used the school as a place for registration; and I'm fairly sure that, as they -- as they found some people in the region, they brought them to the school. Maybe the people were looking for some sort of temporary refuge. With respect to the development in terms of numbers, my memory is pretty hazy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't remember, then I will won't further ask. Also, a document was read to you on which a date was said, where you said then, well, the people had not left the school yet, because you remembered that there was still persons in that school at a later time. That document used the word "released." Could I ask you, where you said you had the impression that it was not a detention situation, that the people were kept there, how you, as I do understand you are a native English speaker, how you understood the use of the term "released" in this respect?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in the early days until the 15th of August, there was this requirement of a propusnica; and, essentially, people were not allowed to leave. So, perhaps, they were detained in a certain way unless they had a safe passage document. After that, I seem to recall that, as long as the authorities did not consider they, you know, had been involved in military activities, that they were free to leave. So when I say "released," I think that term refers more to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness could first finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it refers more to being released essentially from any suspicion that they posed a threat, and therefore they were free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this what you think or do you have any specific reason to believe that, because there -- but perhaps you finished your answer. First, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify. I think the word thinks that you were using the word as if it was his word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not his word. It was a word used in the documents in which I asked you how you understood that word, because the word "released" was used in relation to a certain date. This was expected that they would be released by, I think it was the 15th or 14th. Was that clear to you when I put the question to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I may have misunderstood, Your Honour, and I'm afraid that my recollection is not that clear about the circumstances under which people could have left that facility. I think some people wished to remain for a certain period of time because of security fears or other concerns. I'm probably not your best source of information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we should seek a better source of information. Finally, do you know whether there was those who had not had, in the earlier years, Croatian nationality, so let's say the people that moved in after Croatia had lost control over that territory, would they also receive free passage to the place, villages, hamlets, where they lived before, or would safe passage would be restricted in any way? I'm now talking about - and I saw on the list that, from what I've seen, they were all Serbs - those who had not lived prior to the start of the war earlier in that area. I mean, did they get a safe passage to go back to the villages where they had lived; legally or not is not something are give any opinion about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish I could answer that question, but I really don't think I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, then you can't answer that question. Thank you very much. Have the questions of the Bench raised any further questions for which we could have a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thirty seconds, Your Honour. I just wish to reserve on the record you commented that you believe that all the people on the list were Serbs, and I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I didn't state it, as I said "from what I've seen." I went through the first page, and I only saw Serbs. It's not clear on my recollection, but I went right to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll point that out later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see how I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 105, Your Honours, lines 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to move back today to today's transcript you said 105, line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I said, and I saw on the list that, and I meant to say, "from what I've seen there," I already reserved ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not having fully checked the list for nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no further questions, Ms. Mahindaratne. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Flynn, this concludes your testimony in court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague, and for having answered questions of the parties and of the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again, and I'm glad that this is on Friday and not on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Flynn out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the parties received an MFI list, which I must admit that I have not prepared the MFI list as I usually do, that is, having a clear view on every single document; but, nevertheless, we'll try to make it shorter. D11 was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you had asked for a B/C/S version, and I'm advised that it's updated now with a B/C/S version and is now in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that's correct, and there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. D11 is admitted into evidence. D13, the first comparative video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Was there any issue about transcripts? There was not. Then D13 is admitted into evidence. D14 is similar; another comparative video clip. I think the first one was about broken glass. The second one was about shell impact and police cars or at least cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that, no, there's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D14 is admitted into evidence. Then we move on to D17, filming positions and movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a couple of -- let me just say there's no substantive objection to that. Mr. Misetic and I have discussed that, and just two issues that I can recall. One is that that document was going to be amended as reflected at, I think, page 966 of the transcript? I'm assured that will happen, but that's the only current problem. Secondly, there was going to be -- well, Mr. Misetic and I agreed that there was the need for a clarification about the time reflected on the video. Mr. Misetic can explain that to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are we at a stage where it's right for admission or are we still --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think the amendment does actually require some change to the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll reserve it and fix it this weekend, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D17 is still on our list. D18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, only with the exception that it's another document that I think requires a change in the description of the -- sorry, that the document itself doesn't require anything, and only a change of the description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The description has been changed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Description has been changed and no objection, so D18 is now in evidence. D24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a document that we have been provided the original for a moment, and we will immediately transfer it to the translation unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that still remains on our list until we have received it, until there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. As regards to D25, we have been already provided the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has it been uploaded into e-court, the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution had an opportunity to look at it? It's the one where the date where the witness visited churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did, and there's -- I did confirm that. There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D25 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe Your Honour indicated that you were awaiting a B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, it's still on our list. Thank you for your assistance. I think the same was true for D64, is that correct, regarding the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So it's ready to admit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We'll have further to consider it. I mean, if a video is English spoken, usually we find it not enough that there's just a transcript of the translation, but also the transcript of the spoken word. So, therefore, perhaps for D64, not for any matter of substance, but rather for purposes of procedure, I'd like to leave that on the list for a second, so that we can consider whether we, nevertheless, need a transcript in the original language spoken. D65, if someone could remind me why it's not immediately admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It just needed a number, Your Honour, and I forgot to ask for it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D65, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D65 is admitted into evidence. D67, the video from the Knin reception centre there. We also had transcript issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that remains on our list. We move on to the P numbers. P23. I haven't got all the exhibits here with me; otherwise, I would have been better prepared. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger will take this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with respect to P23, I understand, from discussions with Mr. Misetic, there's -- there was an objection with respect to page 2 of that exhibit. That document relates to a schedule killing. We had already advised the Defence that there were some witness-related issues in connection with that schedule killing. The suggestion was that we defer tendering of this document until such time as witness evidence related to that schedule killing was adduced, and we agree with that suggestion if it meets the satisfaction of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The list is too long to finish it at this moment, as we are quarter to 2.00. However, I advised parties, especially in relation to your last remark, Mr. Tieger, that I scheduled a meeting early next week with the with Mr. Monkhouse and Mr. Nilsson, in order to see how we can keep these MFI numbers short and what to do with the documents which for whatever reason can't be admitted at a certain moment. It might be that once we have finished this conversation, that we further need to speak with the parties. It could also be that we come to conclusions and then the parties will be informed about those conclusions. We'll therefore stop for the day. Mr. Registrar, we are sitting next week in the morning hours, so I take it that, yes, we will adjourn until Monday, the 14th of April, in courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of April, 2008 at 9.00 a.m.
